newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria students vow to remain vigilant.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria students vow to remain vigilant.

text.p: Bulgaria's students, who suspended daily protests after the ruling Socialists agreed to call early elections, vowed on Thursday to remain vigilant and insist the country's leaders implement economic reforms.

"After 30 days of protests we have become an important social and political factor. All politicians understand they have to respect us," said Kamen Petrov from the Coordination of Students and Lecturers Committee.
The students won the hearts of many and the contempt of the Socialists with 30 days of enthusiastic marches through central Sofia.
Each march had a theme, with students roped together as slaves, playing cards with signs saying "The Game's Over", or staging "Miss Protest" contests.
Petrov said: "We cannot stop now. This is just the start of a very difficult process of reform and students want to play an active role in this process."
Opposition leader Ivan Kostov, who led the coalition which drove out the Socialists, paid homage to the students' role in his remarks to a final victory rally after elections were set.
In an obvious appeal to young voters ahead of April's vote, he thanked everyone "and especially the students without whose enthusiasm we wouldn't have gone so far".
Students kept their marches separate from the opposition and their leaders said they supported no particular party, just Bulgaria and the dire need for economic reforms.
At news conferences on Thursday, students said they would keep their protest committees intact to be ready should the politicians fail to deliver.
Now aware of their public image, groups of students turned out on Thursday to clear away debris from roadblocks thrown up around the capital at the height of the protests.

"We are a pressure group and we will be ready to go back in the streets if the politicians forget their promises and start their games again ... we have had enough of lies already," said student leader Petar Haralampiev.
After watching the country's politicians haggle for months while the economy collapsed, the students are wary of joining any single camp.

"The truth is that all politicians want to use the students and their emotional rallies to promote their positions and to use us as the nice young face of their shady political deals", Avram Stanishev from the National Students Protest Committee (NSPC) told Reuters.
NSPC has hammered out a set of demands for securing jobs for students and reforms to the educational system.

"We hope all political parties will include our demands in their pre-election campaign," Stanishev said. "We aren't likely to join any campaign but some students are tempted by promises of an easy political career in the future."
